reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: Presents acutely with abdominal pain or is discovered chronically as cavernous transformation (portal cavernoma) with periportal collaterals.
Cirrhosis is the commonest predisposing factor in adults; other causes include myeloproliferative neoplasms, abdominal sepsis, pancreatitis and malignancy.
Distinguish bland thrombus from tumour thrombus (hepatocellular carcinoma): tumour thrombus expands the vein, enhances arterially and may show pulsatile flow on Doppler.
Extension into the mesenteric veins is the feared complication, risking intestinal congestion, ischaemia and infarction.
Doppler ultrasound is first line; contrast CT or MR portography defines the extent and mesenteric involvement.
Anticoagulation promotes recanalisation and prevents extension in acute non-cirrhotic disease, balanced against variceal bleeding risk after endoscopic assessment.
In non-cirrhotic patients, screen for an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm including JAK2 V617F even when the standard thrombophilia screen is negative.
Chronic portal cavernoma causes portal hypertension with varices and splenomegaly but relatively preserved hepatic synthetic function when non-cirrhotic.
reference.pathophysiology: Thrombosis within the extrahepatic portal vein or its intrahepatic branches arises from the elements of Virchow's triad: reduced portal flow (cirrhosis and portal hypertension), endothelial injury (inflammation, tumour invasion, sclerotherapy, surgery) and hypercoagulability (myeloproliferative neoplasms, inherited or acquired thrombophilias, pregnancy and oestrogen exposure). Obstruction raises portal pressure and, when persistent, drives the development of periportal venous collaterals termed cavernous transformation. If thrombus propagates into the superior mesenteric vein, venous congestion of the bowel can progress to ischaemia and transmural infarction.
additionalDifferentials: Tumour (hepatocellular carcinoma) invasion of the portal vein
Nodular regenerative hyperplasia or idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension
Constrictive pericarditis or cardiac cirrhosis causing portal hypertension
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasonography of the portal venous system
Contrast-enhanced CT or MR portography to map thrombus extent
Full blood count and JAK2 V617F mutation testing
Thrombophilia screen (protein C and S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation)
Liver function and synthetic markers with cause-specific liver workup
Alpha-fetoprotein and cross-sectional imaging to exclude hepatocellular carcinoma
redFlags: Severe worsening abdominal pain with lactic acidosis suggesting mesenteric ischaemia
Peritonism or clinical signs of bowel infarction
New ascites with fever suggesting concurrent sepsis
reference.prognosis: Acute non-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis has a good outcome with prompt anticoagulation and high recanalisation rates, whereas chronic cavernoma carries a risk of portal hypertensive bleeding but usually preserved liver function. Thrombosis complicating cirrhosis or malignancy portends a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Mistaking bland thrombus for tumour thrombus, or vice versa, which fundamentally alters management
Withholding anticoagulation for fear of varices without first assessing and prophylaxing them
Missing mesenteric extension and impending bowel infarction
Overlooking an occult myeloproliferative neoplasm when the standard thrombophilia screen is negative
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Baveno consensus workshop on portal hypertension
management: Anticoagulation, initially low-molecular-weight heparin transitioning to an oral agent, for acute non-cirrhotic thrombosis to promote recanalisation and prevent propagation
Treatment of the underlying cause, including a myeloproliferative neoplasm or thrombophilia, with haematology involvement
Endoscopic screening for varices and appropriate prophylaxis before or alongside anticoagulation to mitigate bleeding risk
Distinction of bland from tumour thrombus, with hepatocellular carcinoma directed therapy where tumour invasion is present
Urgent surgical assessment for mesenteric extension threatening bowel viability, with systemic anticoagulation, possible thrombolysis or thrombectomy, and resection of infarcted bowel
Broad-spectrum antibiotics when septic thrombophlebitis of the portal vein is present
Management of established portal hypertension in chronic cavernoma
